title: Senior's toolkit: debugging loops
summary: Hit counts, logpoints, run to cursor, pausing a hung program and timing a loop.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: debugging loops
steps.body: Loops fail in three ways: they stop one step early or late, they never stop, or they are too slow. These are the tools for each.

toolkit.what: Stop only on the Nth time a line runs, so you can look at iteration 999 without pressing F5 998 times.
flags: right-click the breakpoint > Conditions > Hit Count
right-click the gutter > Add Conditional Breakpoint > Hit Count
toolkit.when: the bug shows up late in a long loop

toolkit.what: A breakpoint that prints a message instead of stopping. You get a log of every pass without editing or rebuilding the code.
flags: breakpoint Settings > Actions; values go in braces: `i={i} sum={sum}`

toolkit.what: Run until the line the cursor is on, for example the line just after the loop, and stop there. A temporary breakpoint you do not have to clean up.
flags: right-click the line > Run to Cursor
toolkit.example: Cursor on the line after the loop, Ctrl+F10, read `count` in Locals

toolkit.what: Stop a program that is stuck. The debugger shows the exact line that is running, which is usually inside the loop that never ends.
flags: then read the loop variable to see why the exit condition never becomes true
toolkit.example: Ctrl+Alt+Break, then F10 a few times to watch `i`
toolkit.when: the app hangs and a CPU core is at 100%

toolkit.what: In the terminal, stop a runaway console program. It is the first thing to press when `dotnet run` never returns.
flags: a program stopped this way does not exit with 0, so scripts can tell

toolkit.what: Measure how long a loop really takes before you guess why it is slow. It lives in `System.Diagnostics`.
flags: the time as a whole number of ms
time with `dotnet run -c Release`; Debug builds are slower

steps.prompt: You run `dotnet run`. Nothing is printed, the fan spins up and the program never ends. What do you do first?
options: Run it under the debugger, press Break All (Pause), and read the loop variable on the line it stopped at
Add more `Console.WriteLine` lines before the loop
steps.explain: A hang with 100% CPU is almost always a loop whose exit condition never becomes true. Pausing shows you which loop, and Locals shows why: often the variable is never changed, or it steps past the end value (`i += 2` with `i != 9`).

steps.prompt: Match each tool to the loop problem it solves.
pairs: print each pass without editing code
jump to the line after the loop
measure how slow the loop really is

steps.prompt: A classic boundary check. What does this print?
steps.explain: `<= 3` includes 3, so four passes. The `while` stops at the first value that is not below 10: 0, 3, 6, 9, 12. Checking the first and last pass like this is what a hit-count breakpoint does for you in a big loop.

steps.prompt: Which tool do you reach for?
items: The import never finishes and one CPU core is at 100%
The program is stuck and you do not know which loop
The total goes wrong somewhere after row 5,000
You want to inspect the last pass of a 10,000-pass loop
The report takes 40 seconds and you need to know which loop is slow
You want to compare two versions of a loop

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: For every loop, check the first and the last pass, either by hand or with a hit-count breakpoint. When something hangs, pause it before you reread it. When something is slow, time it before you change it.
